blocks.heading: 3.6 A Lot & A Little — كتير وشويّة | ktīr w-shwayye
paragraphs: You've learned nouns, adjectives, nominal sentences, and possession. You've also encountered connected nouns, such as غُرْفِة النَّوم (ghurfet in-nōm), even though we haven't formally explained that structure yet.
Now you're ready for two useful everyday quantity expressions:
These expressions work differently from regular descriptive adjectives.
Regular adjectives come after the noun and agree with it in gender. When they describe a definite noun, they also normally take الـ.
كْتير and شْوَيّة express quantity or degree, and they don't follow exactly the same patterns as ordinary adjectives.
You'll also notice that شْوَيّة connects directly to the noun after it. Later in this chapter, when we study الإِضافة, you'll understand why this happens.
For now, focus on how these expressions sound and how to use them naturally.

blocks.heading: ktīr | A Lot / Many
paragraphs: When كتير is used with a noun to mean “a lot of / many,” it is flexible in position. Both of the following are natural in Southern Levantine Arabic:
Unlike regular adjectives, which almost always follow the noun, كتير can appear either before or after it. Both orders are common and natural in everyday Southern Levantine Arabic.

blocks.heading: Ktīr As An Adverb
paragraphs: You will also hear it used as an adverb — modifying adjectives or entire statements. This is just as common in everyday speech as using it with nouns.
In these cases, كْتير works like the English word “very.”
When modifying an adjective, it can come before or after it.
Compare:
Both are natural in everyday speech.
Notice that كْتير does not need to change to agree with the person being described. It stays the same whether the adjective is masculine, feminine, or plural.

blocks.heading: Note (footnote 1)
blocks.text: Although ناس “people” is grammatically feminine singular, both ناس كتير and ناس كتيرة are common in Southern Levantine Arabic. ناس كتير is especially frequent in everyday speech, where كتير functions as an invariable quantity word meaning “many/a lot of.” ناس كتيرة reflects regular feminine-singular adjective agreement with ناس. The two forms normally mean the same thing: “many people.”

blocks.heading: shwayye | A Little / Some
paragraphs: When شْوَيّة (shwayye) comes before a noun, it means “a little bit of” or “some.” Unlike كْتير (ktīr), شْوَيّة (shwayye) has a fixed position: it comes before the noun.
Later in this chapter, you will learn the grammar behind this pattern. For now, focus on how it sounds and what it means.
When شْوَيّة (shwayye) connects to the noun after it, the final ة is pronounced like t:
shwayyet, not shwayye
That gives us forms like:
One more thing: شْوَيّة can also precede a definite noun to mean:
“a little bit of the…”
Naturally, this construction is more specific than the indefinite form. Use it when referring to a specific quantity already identified in the conversation.

items.en: a little bit of the money / some of the money
I have just some of the money for the party.

blocks.heading: shwayy as an Adverb
paragraphs: Just like كْتير (ktīr), شْوَيّ (shwayy) can also modify an adjective.
In this role, it means “a little” or “a bit” and can appear before or after the adjective.

items.en: The house is a little far

paragraphs: Notice that شْوَيّ does not change to agree with the adjective.
Unlike شْوَيّة when connected to a noun, there is no final t sound or إضافة construction here.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
كْتير with nouns means: a lot of / many
شْوَيّة with nouns means: a little bit of / some
كْتير is flexible. It can come before or after the noun.
شْوَيّة is stricter. It always comes before the noun and works like an إضافة.
Both words also work as adverbs.
كْتير before or after an adjective means: very
شْوَيّ before or after an adjective means: a little / a bit

blocks.heading: 3.7 The Addition — الإضافة | il-iḍāfa
paragraphs: Let’s talk about one of the most important structures in Arabic. You have already seen it throughout this book — in vocabulary lists, examples, dialogues, and possession structures.
Now it is time to understand how it works.
The word إِضافة (iḍāfa) literally means “addition.” It is the structure Arabic uses to link two nouns together into one close relationship.
In English, we often express this kind of relationship in three ways:

“the house door”
“Ahmad’s book”
“the door of the room”
Arabic does not need a word for “of” or an apostrophe + s.
Instead, it places the two nouns directly next to each other. The relationship between them is understood from word order and context.

No word for “of.”
No apostrophe.
Just two nouns forming one tight unit.
Let’s look at how it works.

blocks.heading: Structure
paragraphs: The إِضافة (iḍāfa) links two nouns to show a close relationship, such as possession, part of a whole, contents, family relationships, or association.
The first noun is the thing we are talking about. This is called the مُضاف (muḍāf).
The second noun tells us more about the first noun. It identifies, describes, or specifies it. This is called the مُضاف إِلَيْه (muḍāf ilayh).
Think of the basic structure as:
[the thing] + [whose / which / what kind]
كتاب (ktāb) is the مُضاف (muḍāf). It is the thing we are talking about: a book.
أَحْمَد (Aḥmad) is the مُضاف إِلَيْه (muḍāf ilayh). It tells us whose book: Ahmad’s.

blocks.heading: The Tāʾ Marbūṭa Rule
paragraphs: You already learned that feminine nouns ending in ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) reveal a hidden t sound when they connect forward. The إِضافة (iḍāfa) is one of the main places where this happens.
When the first noun ends in ة and is followed by the second noun in an إِضافة (iḍāfa), the ة is pronounced with a clear t sound.
You have already seen this happen with شْوَيّة (shwayye).
When شْوَيّة (shwayye) connects to the noun after it, you hear the same t sound:
Earlier, you learned to recognize and use this pattern. Now you know why it happens.
The ة is showing its t sound because the first noun is connected directly to the noun after it.

blocks.heading: Definiteness
paragraphs: Now let’s look at one of the most important rules of the إِضافة (iḍāfa): definiteness. An إِضافة (iḍāfa) can be either definite or indefinite.
The central rule is simple: the definiteness of an إضافة is determined by the final noun in the construction.
When there are only two nouns, this means the second noun.
Compare:
Notice that the first two nouns remain without الـ in each example.
What changes is the final noun. When that noun is definite, the entire إضافة becomes definite.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
The first noun in an إضافة never takes الـ. In a longer إضافة chain, the final noun determines whether the entire phrase is definite or indefinite.
A noun does not need الـ to be definite. Names and possessive suffixes do the same job. That is the next page.

blocks.heading: Proper Names Are Already Definite
paragraphs: If the second noun is a proper name — a person’s name, a city, or a country — you do not need الـ (il-).
There is no الـ (il-) anywhere in these phrases, but they are still definite.
The name itself identifies a specific person and does the job that الـ (il-) would otherwise do..

blocks.heading: Possessive Suffixes Also Make a Noun Definite
paragraphs: You already learned that possessive suffixes make a noun definite.
My house, his book, and her room all refer to specific, definite nouns. When a noun with a possessive suffix appears as the second noun in an إِضافة (iḍāfa), the entire phrase is definite.

items.en: her room door / the door of her room
our house key / the key of our house

paragraphs: Again, the first noun stays without الـ (il-). The second noun is already definite because of its possessive suffix, so the entire إِضافة (iḍāfa) is definite.

blocks.heading: Indefinite iḍāfa | إِضافة
paragraphs: Compare:

items.en: a room door / the door of a room
the room door / the door of the room

paragraphs: In باب غُرفة, غُرفة is indefinite, so the exact room is unknown. Therefore, the entire phrase is indefinite.
In باب الغُرفة, الغُرفة is definite, so we are referring to a specific room. Therefore, the entire phrase is definite.
Example in context:

items.ar: رَح يكون في باب غُرْفِة نَوم بِنُصّ المَمَرّ.
items.translit: raḥ ykūn fī bāb ghurfet nōm b-nuṣṣ il-mamarr
items.en: There will be a bedroom door halfway down the hallway.

paragraphs: Here, the final noun نوم is indefinite, so باب غُرفة نوم refers to a bedroom door, not a specific one already known.

blocks.heading: Where students get tripped up
blocks.text:
With an indefinite iḍāfa, it is easy to focus on the first noun and read باب غُرفة as simply “a door.” It actually means “a door of a room.”
Always read the iḍāfa as a single unit: باب غُرفة = a door belonging to a room

blocks.heading: What Relationships Does the إضافة Express?
paragraphs: Do not think of إِضافة (iḍāfa) as only expressing ownership. It is much broader than that.
Here are some of the most common relationships it expresses:

items.en: the room door / the door of the room
the bedroom / the room for sleeping
the restaurant door / the door of the restaurant
the neighborhood school / the school of the neighborhood

paragraphs: The relationship between the nouns is understood from their meanings, word order, and context.
You do not need an extra word between them. The two nouns form one tight unit.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
The إِضافة (iḍāfa) links two nouns together to form one close relationship.
The first noun is the مُضاف (muḍāf) — the thing you are talking about.
The second noun is the مُضاف إِلَيْه (muḍāf ilayh) — it tells you whose, which, or what kind.
The first noun never takes الـ (il-), and the second noun determines whether the entire phrase is definite or indefinite.
[the thing] + [whose / which / what kind]

lessons.title: Connecting Concepts: The Addition vs. The Demonstrative

blocks.heading: Connecting Concepts — The Addition vs. The Demonstrative
paragraphs: You already know your demonstratives — هادا، هاي، هَداك، هَديك، and so on. Now that you have learned الإِضافَة, you need to know how demonstratives work with an iḍāfa phrase.
The natural, everyday pattern is:
demonstrative + iḍāfa phrase

The demonstrative points to the entire iḍāfa phrase, but it agrees in gender and number with the first noun in the chain — the مُضاف. This is because the first noun is the main noun of the entire phrase.

items.en: this house door / this is the door of the house
items.note: The demonstrative هادا agrees with باب, which is masculine.

items.en: this bedroom / this is the bedroom
items.note: The demonstrative هاي agrees with غُرفة, which is feminine. It does not agree with نَوم, because نَوم is the second noun in the iḍāfa phrase.

items.en: this coffee table / this is the coffee table
this apartment building’s entrance / this is the entrance of the apartment building
this house’s garden / this is the garden of the house

blocks.heading: One Structure, Different Functions
paragraphs: A demonstrative followed by an iḍāfa phrase can function in different ways depending on what comes after it and the context in which it is used.
Compare:

items.en: This is the bedroom. / This bedroom.

paragraphs: These structures look very similar, but they are doing different jobs.

blocks.heading: 1. Demonstrative + Iḍāfa
paragraphs: Two ways to say “this bedroom”
Palestinian Arabic has two word orders for “this bedroom,” and you will hear both:
In both, هاي agrees with غرفة, the first noun. To say something about the bedroom, keep going:

blocks.heading: “This is the bedroom”
paragraphs: هاي غرفة النوم can also be a complete sentence: “This is the bedroom.” Arabic needs no word for “is,” so the words are identical. Word order alone does not always tell you which meaning is intended. Context does.
To make “This is the bedroom” unmistakable, speakers can add هي:
With a masculine noun, use هو:
The same sentences without the extra pronoun are just as correct:
Teachers often call this هو / هي a “pronoun copula.” It is not required. It simply makes the “is” clear.
Imagine someone is showing you around an apartment and you ask:
Here, the phrase identifies the room and can stand as a complete utterance. But imagine several rooms have already been mentioned and someone asks:

items.ar: هاي غُرفة النَّوم أَكْبَر مِن غُرفة الضُّيوف.
items.translit: hāy ghurfet in-nōm akbar min ghurfet iḍ-ḍyūf
items.en: This bedroom is bigger than the guest room.
items.note: You point to the bedroom and say:

paragraphs: Here, هاي غُرفة النَّوم means this bedroom and serves as the topic of a larger sentence.
The Arabic structure itself has not changed. The previous conversation, the shared situation, intonation, and what comes next help determine how the phrase is functioning.

You may have noticed أَكْبَر مِن (akbar min), meaning “bigger than.” This comparative structure will be taught in Volume Two. For now, focus on how the demonstrative works; you only need to understand the comparative, not produce it.

blocks.heading: 2. Demonstrative + Iḍāfa + Indefinite Adjective
paragraphs: When an indefinite adjective follows the iḍāfa phrase, it can function as the predicate of a nominal sentence.
Here:

هاي غُرفة النَّوم = this bedroom
واسِعة = is spacious
The adjective gives new information about the bedroom and completes the nominal sentence.
The same pattern appears in:

items.en: This apartment building’s entrance is narrow.

blocks.heading: 3. Demonstrative + Iḍāfa + Definite Adjective
paragraphs: When a definite adjective follows the iḍāfa phrase and agrees with the first noun, the adjective becomes part of the larger noun phrase.
The adjective الواسِعة describes غُرفة. It is part of the noun phrase and is not functioning as the predicate of a nominal sentence.
When a definite adjective follows an إضافة, it becomes part of the noun phrase rather than functioning as the predicate.
However, this does not necessarily mean the sentence is incomplete.
Compare:

items.note: Here, واسِعة gives new information about the bedroom.
Here, الواسِعة identifies which bedroom we mean.

items.ar: هاي غُرفة النَّوم الواسِعة جَنْب الحَمّام
items.translit: hāy ghurfet in-nōm il-wāsʿa janb il-ḥammām
items.en: This spacious bedroom is next to the bathroom
items.note: Here, جَنْب الحَمّام provides additional information about the spacious bedroom.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
An indefinite adjective can function as the predicate, while a definite adjective becomes part of the noun phrase.
Whether the full expression is a complete statement or part of a longer sentence depends on how it is used.

paragraphs: Here, الواسِعة is part of the noun phrase. The listener will typically expect more information to follow.
Context can sometimes make a noun phrase sufficient by itself, especially as a short answer, correction, contrast, label, or when identifying something that is physically present.
For example:

blocks.heading: Pattern 4: Shifting Focus with Demonstratives
paragraphs: You already learned how demonstratives normally work with إضافة phrases. Here is another useful pattern that lets you change what the demonstrative points to.
The demonstrative can appear in two different positions:

blocks.heading: A. Demonstrative Before the إضافة Phrase
paragraphs: demonstrative + إضافة
This pattern points to the first noun — the thing being discussed.

items.en: This is the room’s window. / This room’s window.
items.note: The demonstrative هاد agrees with شُبّاك, the first noun in the إضافة phrase.

items.en: This is the house’s garden. / This house’s garden.
items.note: The demonstrative هاي agrees with جَنينِة, the first noun.

blocks.heading: B. Demonstrative After the إضافة Phrase
paragraphs: إضافة + demonstrative
After the phrase, the demonstrative agrees with whichever noun it points to.

items.note: (هاي agrees with الغرفة; شبّاك is masculine)
The demonstrative هاي agrees with الغُرفة, not with شُبّاك.
The demonstrative هاد agrees with البَيْت, not with جَنينِة.

blocks.heading: Easy Way to Remember
blocks.text:
Demonstrative before the إضافة = points to the first noun.

blocks.heading: 3.8 Explicit Ownership — تَبَع | tabaʿ
paragraphs: In this chapter, you have already learned several ways to talk about possession and “having” in Southern Levantine Arabic:

• ʿind + suffix for things in your general life
• maʿ + suffix for things with you right now
• ilī / ilak / ilo for saying “this is mine / yours / his”
• the iḍāfa relational construction

We are now ready for the last possession structure in this chapter. Once you add this one, your basic possession toolkit will be complete. You already know possessive suffixes where the last letter or two letters indicates ownership of an object.
They are the shortest way to show ownership. Now let’s add a very common Levantine alternative:

On its own, tabaʿ carries the idea of “belonging to” or “of.” In speech, it works as a small linking word after a noun to show who or what that noun belongs to. Unlike suffixes, it can also agree with the noun in gender and number and then take a pronoun ending to show the owner. تَبَع is a very common way to talk about possession in Levantine Arabic, and you’ll hear it all the time in everyday speech. However, it is governed by certain rules. Take a look at a couple of examples, and see if you can identify what they are:

items.en: My book is in the car.

blocks.heading: The Rules:
paragraphs: 1. The thing being owned should be definite.
In the pattern you are learning here, the noun before تَبَع (tabaʿ) is definite. It will normally have الـ (il-) or a demonstrative such as هادا (hāda) or هاي (hāy).

items.en: the book is mine / my book

paragraphs: 2. تَبَع comes after the noun.
In English, “my” comes first. In this construction, the thing comes first, then ownership:
3. The form changes with the thing, not with the owner
This is important. The owner is shown by the pronoun ending.
But the basic shape changes according to the thing being owned:

masculine thing → تَبَع (tabaʿ)
feminine thing → تَبَعَة (tabaʿa)
plural things → تَبَعون (tabaʿūn)
When تَبَعَة (tabaʿa) is followed by a possessive suffix, the final ـة is pronounced as t, and the form becomes تَبَعِتـ (tabaʿit-).
So:
Compare:
The owner can change, but the basic form still agrees with the thing being owned:
The noun الكِتاب (il-ktāb) is masculine singular, so the form remains based on تَبَع (tabaʿ).
The noun السَّيّارَة (is-sayyāra) is feminine singular, so the form is based on تَبَعَة (tabaʿa), which becomes تَبَعِتـ (tabaʿit-) before a suffix.
The noun الأَواعي (il-awāʿi) is plural, so the form is based on تَبَعون (tabaʿūn).

blocks.heading: 4. تَبَع (tabaʿ) is followed by a possessive pronoun (suffix) to show ownership
paragraphs: The possessive suffix shows who the owner is. The form of تَبَع (tabaʿ), تَبَعَة (tabaʿa), or تَبَعون (tabaʿūn) has already been chosen according to the thing being owned. Then, the appropriate possessive suffix is added.

blocks.heading: Usage
paragraphs: OK… that was a lot of rules, but don’t worry – it is much easier in practice. Let’s look at some usage to get a feel for how it works.

blocks.heading: Simple possession
paragraphs: Most of the time, this structure gives you a clear, natural way to say my / your / his / her / our / their with a specific noun.

items.en: my book / the book is mine
her car / the car is hers

blocks.heading: A Small but Important Difference
paragraphs: تَبَع and possessive suffixes can express similar meanings, but they do not always function the same way.
Compare:
The first is a possessed noun. The second can function as a complete sentence identifying ownership.
In everyday speech, both can help identify something as belonging to someone. The difference is how they fit into the sentence.

items.en: her car / the car is hers

blocks.heading: Asking “Whose?”
paragraphs: To ask “Whose?”, use:
Put it after a definite noun:

blocks.heading: “Belonging to” or “of”
paragraphs: You can also use this structure to connect one noun to another similar to an iḍāfa. In addition, if adding a possessive pronoun suffix to the Iḍāfa structure sounds awkward or is unclear, then this structure can be used to clear up ambiguity or make speech faster and easier.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
Start with the definite thing being owned.
الكِتاب (il-ktāb)
السَّيّارَة (is-sayyāra)
الأَواعي (il-awāʿi)
Match تَبَع (tabaʿ) to the thing being owned.
Masculine singular → تَبَع (tabaʿ)
الكِتاب تَبَعي | my book – il-ktāb tabaʿī
Feminine singular → تَبَعِت / تَبَعَة (tabaʿit / tabaʿa)
السَّيّارَة تَبَعِتها | her car – is-sayyāra tabaʿitha
Plural → تَبَعون (tabaʿūn)
الأَواعي تَبَعوني | my clothes – il-awāʿi tabaʿūni
Add the owner after the correct form of تَبَع (tabaʿ).
The owner can be a pronoun suffix, such as تَبَعي (tabaʿī), تَبَعَك (tabaʿak), تَبَعها (tabaʿha), or تَبَعنا (tabaʿna).
The owner can also be another noun, such as تَبَع المُدير (tabaʿ il-mudīr).
Formula:
[Definite Thing] + [Correct تَبَع (tabaʿ) Form] + [Owner]
المَكْتَب تَبَع المُدير | the manager’s office – il-maktab tabaʿ il-mudīr

blocks.heading: Putting It All Together
paragraphs: In this chapter, you learned how to move from simply naming things to showing where they are, what exists, who has something, who something belongs to, and how objects relate to the space around them. This is a major step because Arabic now starts to feel less like isolated words and more like real description.
Here are the main structures:

blocks.heading: في / ما في = there is / there isn’t

items.en: There is a book on the table.
There is no bag behind the door.

blocks.heading: Prepositions and locatives = where something is

paragraphs: Now watch these pieces come together in a short, natural conversation. As always, there may be some vocabulary that you don’t know, but that’s okay. You’ll be learning it shortly. Our next step is learning how to express desire.

blocks.heading: Ghayda’s New Place | شقة غيداء الجديدة
paragraphs: This final activity reviews all the key grammar and vocabulary from Chapter 3 (prepositions & locatives, fī/mā fī, ḥatta, human/non-human possession, iḍāfa, tabaʿ, adjectives, etc.). It also gives you a taste of the natural conversational style you’ll see in the next chapter.

blocks.heading: Picture the Scene
blocks.text:
Ghayda is moving out of her parents’ house and into her own apartment near the university. The apartment is already fully furnished, so she does not need to buy any furniture. It has two furnished bedrooms, a spacious living room, a large kitchen, and a balcony with a beautiful view. Everything is organized and ready for her, and tonight she is having people over to see her new place.
In the first scene, Ghayda and her friend Walaa are talking on the phone. In the second scene, Walaa visits Ghayda’s new apartment for the first time.

blocks.heading: A New Apartment
paragraphs: There are a few expressions in Ghayda and Walaa’s conversation that are worth taking a closer look at. Some are useful for describing a home, while others are things you’ll hear in everyday conversations that don’t always translate neatly into English.
Let’s start with Walaa’s reaction when she sees the apartment.

items.en: Wow! The apartment is really nice!

paragraphs: يا سَلام is a common expression of surprise, admiration, or excitement. Here, Walaa is impressed by the apartment.

You might hear the same expression when someone shows you something beautiful, tells you some good news, or surprises you with something unexpected. The meaning depends quite a bit on the speaker’s tone.

blocks.heading: لَحالِك — On your own
paragraphs: Walaa also asks:

items.en: Is this your first apartment of your own?

paragraphs: The important expression here is لَحالِك, meaning “on your own” or “by yourself.”
Walaa wants to know whether this is Ghayda’s first place of her own. The expression adds that extra detail without requiring a whole separate sentence.

blocks.heading: شِكْل العَفِش — The furniture looks
paragraphs: Later, Walaa comments on the furniture:
Notice the word شِكْل. It literally relates to appearance or form, but here it’s being used to describe how something looks.
This is a useful expression because we often describe things based on what we can see rather than what we know for certain.
We’ll spend more time with شِكْلـ in Chapter 5, so there’s no need to worry about all its different forms just yet.

blocks.heading: إِلها إِطْلالِة — It has a view
paragraphs: When Walaa asks about the balcony, Ghayda says:

items.ar: إِلها إِطْلالِة كْتير حِلْوِة عَ المَدينة.
items.en: It has a really beautiful view of the city.

paragraphs: The word إِطْلالِة refers to a view or outlook, especially from a balcony, window, or building.
And notice how Ghayda uses إِلها. She’s talking about the balcony, so she’s saying that it has a beautiful view.
It’s a good example of how a familiar possession structure can be used to describe something beyond physical ownership.

blocks.heading: A Few More Things Worth Noticing
paragraphs: Toward the end of the conversation, Walaa congratulates Ghayda on her new apartment. This brings us to an expression you’ll hear all the time.
مَبْروك is used for all kinds of happy occasions: a new home, a wedding, a new job, a graduation, or just about anything worth celebrating.
Ghayda responds:
This is a common response to مَبْروك. Since Ghayda is speaking to Walaa, she uses فيكي, the feminine form.

blocks.heading: حَتّى — Even
paragraphs: Ghayda also mentions that her new neighbors are coming to the gathering:

items.en: Even the new neighbors are invited.

paragraphs: Here, حَتّى means “even.” It draws attention to something that might be a little surprising or unexpected.
It’s a small word, but it can change the emphasis of an entire sentence.
